title: Floating-Point Values and Decimal Precision
learningObjectives: Distinguish float, double and long double floating types.
Explain why many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point.
Use suitable printf precision to inspect floating-point values.
Compare calculated floating-point values using a justified tolerance when appropriate.
Recognize range, precision, rounding and non-finite-value considerations.

understand.concept: C provides float, double and long double floating types. Many decimal fractions have no finite binary representation, so stored values are approximations and arithmetic can introduce rounding error. Precision and range depend on the implementation. Exact equality is often inappropriate after floating-point calculations; the comparison method should reflect the scale and error tolerance of the problem.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding precision is important for measurements, scientific calculations and money-like values. A program must choose an appropriate representation and comparison strategy rather than assuming decimal fractions are exact.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Floating-point type choices

float, double and long double provide floating-point representations with different ranges and precision characteristics. double is commonly used for general calculations. The actual characteristics are described by `<float.h>`.

## 2. Decimal values are often approximations

A value such as 0.1 cannot be represented exactly with a finite binary fraction. Therefore `0.1 + 0.2` may not have exactly the same stored value as the literal 0.3. Printing more digits can reveal the approximation.

## 3. Display precision

printf uses `%f`, `%e` or `%g` for floating-point output. A precision such as `%.2f` controls the number of digits after the decimal point for `%f`; it changes the displayed representation, not the stored value.

## 4. Compare with a tolerance

For many numerical tasks, compare the absolute difference against a tolerance selected for the problem's scale and required accuracy. A single arbitrary epsilon is not correct for every application. Some problems require exact decimal arithmetic or integer-scaled units instead.

## 5. Handle special values and ranges

Floating-point calculations can produce very large values, infinities or NaNs depending on the operation and implementation. Check domain constraints and use facilities from `<math.h>` when appropriate. Do not assume floating point is suitable for exact financial accounting.

options: The decimal fractions may be approximated in binary floating-point representation
The plus operator always loses one digit
questions.answer: The decimal fractions may be approximated in binary floating-point representation
questions.explanation: Many decimal fractions do not have finite binary representations.
